sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative policies based on diffusion models ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) and flow matching models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for policy learning. Diffusion policies generate actions through iterative denoising, while flow policies generate actions by integrating a learned velocity field, often providing a deterministic and more efficient alternative. Due to their flexibility and accuracy in modeling high-dimensional action distributions, generative policies have achieved strong empirical gains over deterministic or unimodal policies in challenging continuous-control settings ( Ke et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . A natural way to further improve generative policies is through reinforcement learning fine-tuning. However, a central challenge is that the exact likelihoods of generative policies are generally intractable, since each action is produced only after simulating an entire denoising or flow trajectory. This prevents the direct use of many stable and widely adopted policy optimization methods, such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Several recent works have attempted to bypass this likelihood challenge ( Psenka et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; McAllister et al., 2025 ) . However, these methods often suffer from biased estimation, limited data efficiency, substantial computational overhead, or restriction to a particular generative policy class or policy update rule. Consequently, the full potential of RL for diffusion and flow policies remains underexplored. To address this problem, we propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO) , a likelihood-free framework that separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. The first stage represents the desired policy improvement through a target policy ratio. The second stage distills the resulting ratio-tilted target into the generative policy. This decomposition avoids evaluating the likelihood of the generative policy itself. The policy-improvement stage is agnostic to the underlying generative model and accommodates a broad family of updates, including regularized Policy Mirror Descent ( Zhan et al., 2023 ) , Soft Actor-Critic ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) , PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . The generative stage uses Doob’s h h -transform to characterize the ratio-tilted target process and learns this process through Doob’s Drift Matching. The same construction applies to both diffusion and flow policies. Contributions. Our contributions are three-fold: • Method. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO) , a unified framework for RL fine-tuning of generative policies without evaluating exact action likelihoods ( Section 3 ). DoobPO follows a two-stage design: it first obtains the target policy ratio and then transfers the resulting policy improvement into the generative policy through a tractable conditional drift matching objective. The framework supports both diffusion and flow policies ( Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). We summarize the procedures in Algorithms 1 and 2 . Instantiating DoobPO with different policy updates yields DoobPMD , DoobPPO , and DoobGRPO . We further show that several existing methods arise as special cases under particular choices of the policy update and generative policy class ( Section 3.3 ). We summarize these instantiations in Table 1 . • Theory. We characterize the ratio-tilted target policy through Doob’s h h -transform ( Lemma 3.1 ). This characterization leads to Doob’s Drift Matching as a principled way to realize the desired policy update. For tractability, we introduce a conditional drift matching objective and prove that its gradient is proportional to that of the ideal Doob’s Drift Matching objective for both diffusion and flow policies ( Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 ). From the Stochastic Optimal Control perspective ( Section 3.4 ), we further show that the Doob-transformed diffusion solves the corresponding endpoint-constrained control problem ( Proposition 3.1 ). Hence, DoobPO learns the minimum-energy modification of the pretrained diffusion process that realizes the terminal tilt ( Remark 3.2 ). • Experiments. We evaluate DoobPO on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks with both diffusion and flow policies ( Section 4 ). For diffusion policies, DoobPO achieves the strongest overall performance against competitive diffusion-policy RL baselines, with leading results on most tasks ( Section 4.2 ). For flow policies, DoobGRPO achieves the best performance on 9 out of 10 tasks under the same interaction budget and delivers large gains on challenging locomotion environments ( Section 4.3 ). These results establish DoobPO as a strong and practical framework for RL fine-tuning across both diffusion and flow policies. Notation. We summarize notation and time conventions in Appendix A . Related Work. We defer an extended discussion of related work to Appendix B due to page limits.

sections.heading: 3 Likelihood-Free Generative Policy Optimization
sections.text: We introduce Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO) , a general framework for RL fine-tuning of diffusion policies ( Section 3.1 ) and flow policies ( Section 3.2 ) without evaluating exact action likelihoods. DoobPO supports a broad family of trust-region policy gradient methods, while Section 3.3 shows how both existing and proposed algorithms arise under the same framework.

sections.heading: 3.3 Unified Framework and Instantiations
sections.text: DoobPO is a unified framework with two design choices. The first is the generative policy class. The second is the policy update method that specifies the target policy improvement. Different choices along these two dimensions induce a broad family of diffusion/flow matching RL algorithms. Under this view, several prior methods arise as special cases of DoobPO. In particular, they correspond to policy updates that admit closed-form solutions. In these cases, the ratio-learning stage becomes unnecessary, and DoobPO reduces to a single reweighted drift matching step. For example, DPMD ( Ma et al., 2025 ) corresponds to a policy update with an analytic target ratio. Under a KL-proximal policy mirror descent update ( Zhan et al., 2023 ) , the updated policy satisfies π ⁡ ( a | o ) ∝ π old ​ ( a | o ) ​ exp ⁡ ( A ^ old ​ ( o , a ) / λ ) \pi(a|o)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a|o)\exp(\hat{A}_{\mathrm{old}}(o,a)/\lambda) . Therefore, the corresponding probability ratio satisfies r ⁡ ( o , a ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( A ^ old ​ ( o , a ) / λ ) r(o,a)\propto\exp(\hat{A}_{\mathrm{old}}(o,a)/\lambda) . For more general trust-region policy-gradient methods such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , the target ratio does not admit a closed form. DoobPO then learns a lightweight ratio model and distills the resulting policy improvement into the generative policy through drift matching. In this work, we derive DoobPPO and DoobGRPO for both diffusion policies and flow policies by instantiating the RL update with PPO and GRPO. Hence, the same framework covers both prior closed-form methods and our new learned-ratio instantiations. We summarize representative examples in Table 1 .

sections.heading: Diffusion Policy Results.
sections.text: Table 2 and Figure 1 report the diffusion-policy results. Overall, DoobPO achieves the highest mean returns among diffusion-policy RL methods on 8 out of 10 MuJoCo tasks, including ties. DoobPPO obtains the best results on HalfCheetah, Humanoid, and Swimmer, while DoobGRPO performs best on Reacher and Pusher. Both variants achieve competitive performance on the remaining tasks, while DACER obtains the highest returns on Ant and Hopper. Compared with DIPO, DoobPPO improves performance by 22.6% on HalfCheetah, 20.9% on Humanoid, 175.2% on Ant, and 12.2% on Walker2d. It also improves over DPMD by 18.3%, 30.0%, 6.0%, and 4.9% on the same tasks, respectively. Against SDAC, DoobPPO achieves gains of 8.2% on Humanoid, 8.8% on Hopper, and 8.9% on Walker2d. The strong performance of DoobGRPO on Reacher and Pusher further demonstrates that the framework is not limited to a single PPO-style instantiation. Together, these results establish DoobPO as a competitive and flexible framework for diffusion-policy RL.

sections.heading: Flow Policy Results.
sections.text: Table 3 and Figure 2 report the flow-policy results. Overall, DoobGRPO achieves the strongest performance across the MuJoCo benchmark under the same 5M-step training budget, obtaining the best results on 9 out of 10 tasks (including ties). Compared with prior flow-policy RL baselines, DoobGRPO gives large gains on key locomotion tasks. For example, it improves over the strongest baseline ReinFlow by 373.8% on HalfCheetah , 71.7% on Hopper , 213.7% on Swimmer , and 738.0% on Walker2d . On the manipulation tasks, DoobGRPO also achieves the best performance on Reacher and Pusher , improving over ReinFlow by 42.9% and 9.0% . DoobPMD serves as a strong second-best on several tasks, including HalfCheetah , Reacher , and Humanoid . This further demonstrates the generality of the DoobPO framework across different policy-gradient methods. These results show that DoobPO provides a useful RL framework for flow policies.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: To evaluate DoobPO beyond MuJoCo continuous control, we test it on the Can and Square manipulation tasks from Robomimic ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) . Both tasks use low-dimensional state observations, sparse binary success rewards, and an action-chunk horizon of 4. The maximum episode lengths are 300 primitive steps for Can and 400 for Square . We follow the official Robomimic evaluation protocol with 50 parallel environments. An episode is successful if the binary task-completion reward is achieved at least once, and the success rate is computed over all completed evaluation episodes. We compare DoobPPO with DPPO ( Ren et al., 2024 ) . Both methods are initialized from the same pretrained diffusion behavior-cloning policy and trained for 151 iterations on Can and 200 iterations on Square , and results are averaged over 3 random seeds. The DoobPPO hyperparameters are listed in Table 6 .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: DoobPPO matches or slightly improves upon DPPO on both tasks, reaching success rates of 99.46% versus 99.23% on Can and 99.78% versus 99.59% on Square . Since both tasks are close to saturation, the main takeaway is not a large performance gap but that DoobPO extends to sparse-reward manipulation settings.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduce Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO) , a unified framework for RL fine-tuning of diffusion and flow policies. The framework supports a broad family of policy updates and avoids exact action-likelihood evaluation by separating policy improvement from generative policy learning. Theoretically, we justify DoobPO from two directions. First, we characterize the ratio-tilted diffusion process through Doob’s h h -transform ( Lemma 3.1 ). We then show that, for each fixed state, the gradient of the conditional drift matching objective is proportional to that of the ideal objective for both diffusion and flow policies ( Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 ). Second, under the stated assumptions, the population minimizer of conditional drift matching induces a diffusion process that solves the corresponding endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem ( Proposition 3.1 ). The resulting process is the minimum-energy modification of the reference diffusion that realizes the prescribed tilted endpoint marginals. This provides a control-theoretic interpretation of how the desired policy update is transferred into generative dynamics. Experimentally, we evaluate DoobPO on MuJoCo benchmarks with both diffusion and flow policies and observe superior overall performance against strong baselines ( Sections 4.2 and 4.3 ). More broadly, DoobPO provides a common interface between policy optimization and generative model training. Policy updates with analytic ratios and updates represented by learned ratio models are accommodated within the same conditional drift matching framework ( Section 3.3 ). This separates the choice of the policy update rule from the choice of the generative policy class. Nevertheless, our study mainly focuses on continuous generation, and the empirical evaluation is limited to MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks and Robomimic manipulation tasks. The theoretical results characterize population objectives under the stated assumptions. An important direction for future work is to quantify how ratio estimation error and approximate drift matching affect the realized policy update. We also plan to extend the framework to discrete generation and evaluate its applicability to more complex policy learning settings.

sections.heading: Diffusion Model and Diffusion Policy.
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) are probabilistic generative models that progressively transform noise into samples from a target distribution. They are closely connected to score-based generative modeling ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , which offers a complementary view based on learning the gradient field of the data distribution and unifies diffusion-based generation under the stochastic differential equation framework. Owing to their strong expressiveness for complex, high-dimensional, and multimodal distributions, diffusion models have become increasingly attractive for control and decision-making. In particular, diffusion policies parameterize action distributions with diffusion models and generate actions through iterative denoising, yielding richer policy classes than standard unimodal Gaussian actors. Prior work has shown strong empirical performance of diffusion policies in visuomotor control and robotic manipulation ( Chi et al., 2025 ) , as well as in goal-conditioned imitation learning and language- or play-conditioned skill learning ( Reuss et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . More recently, diffusion policies have been extended to online reinforcement learning. Methods such as DPPO and related diffusion-policy RL approaches show that diffusion-based policy classes can be optimized effectively beyond pure imitation learning ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Our work builds on this line of research, but focuses on RL fine-tuning of diffusion policies in the likelihood-intractable setting. We compare against five recent diffusion-policy RL baselines: DIPO ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , DPPO ( Ren et al., 2024 ) , DPMD ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , DACER ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and SDAC ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . These baselines cover both off-policy and on-policy diffusion RL methods: DIPO, DPMD, DACER, and SDAC are off-policy, whereas DPPO is on-policy. DIPO adopts a two-stage strategy that first updates state-action particles using value gradients and then distills them into a diffusion policy. DPPO formulates policy optimization over a diffusion-augmented MDP and applies Proximal Policy Optimization to the resulting process. DPMD studies efficient online RL for diffusion policies through a policy-mirror-descent-style update with an analytic target ratio. DACER directly backpropagates value gradients through the reverse diffusion process and introduces entropy regularization to improve exploration. SDAC extends diffusion-policy optimization to the soft-actor-critic regime with an analytic-ratio-based update. Our work generalizes the analytic-ratio ideas underlying DPMD and SDAC into a unified likelihood-free framework, extending them from diffusion policies to flow matching policies and to a broader class of policy optimization methods, including PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Flow Matching Model and Flow Policy.
sections.text: Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) provides an alternative to diffusion models by learning a deterministic ODE transport between a noise prior and the data distribution. Compared to diffusion models, flow matching avoids simulating stochastic dynamics during training and offers faster sampling through fewer integration steps. These properties have made flow matching models increasingly popular in decision-making applications. π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) and its successor π 0.5 ∗ \pi_{0.5}^{*} ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ) adopt flow matching as the generative backbone of vision-language-action models for general robot manipulation, demonstrating that flow policies can scale to diverse real-world tasks. However, the likelihood of a flow policy is as intractable as that of a diffusion policy, since it requires solving an ODE and computing the associated log-determinant of the Jacobian. This intractability poses the same challenge for online RL fine-tuning: standard policy gradient methods that rely on likelihood ratios cannot be directly applied. Flow Q-Learning ( Park et al., 2025 ) is an early attempt that sidesteps this issue by using Q-function guidance to steer the flow sampling process, analogous to Q-guided diffusion methods. For policy gradient approaches, several workarounds have been proposed. FPO ( McAllister et al., 2025 ) is a PPO-style method that replaces explicit policy ratios with an implicit surrogate derived from the flow matching training loss, avoiding likelihood computation entirely. ReinFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) converts a deterministic flow policy into a stochastic short-horizon Markov process via learned noise injection, enabling tractable stepwise likelihood computation for policy gradient updates. Flow-SDE ( Chen et al., 2025 ) instead replaces the deterministic flow ODE with an analytically constructed stochastic differential equation, yielding explicit transition probabilities suitable for policy gradient estimation. All these methods require some form of likelihood evaluation or surrogate at the denoising steps; in contrast, our approach bypasses this requirement entirely by learning a lightweight ratio network that directly estimates the probability ratio needed for policy optimization.

sections.heading: G.3 Ratio Regularizer in the Off-Policy Setting
sections.text: In the on-policy variant, the ratio centering regularizer enforces 𝔼 a ′ ∼ π old ( ⋅ | o ) [ r β ( o , a ′ ) ] ≈ 1 \mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(\cdot|o)}[r_{\beta}(o,a^{\prime})]\approx 1 by sampling actions from the frozen rollout policy, which corresponds exactly to the normalization constraint of the density ratio. In the off-policy variant with a replay buffer, there is no single well-defined behavior policy associated with each stored transition, since the buffer aggregates experience from many past policy versions. We therefore estimate the centering constraint by sampling a ′ a^{\prime} from the current actor at the same state o o . This ensures that the learned ratio remains well-calibrated within the support of the evolving policy, effectively regularizing r β r_{\beta} against degenerate solutions regardless of the age of the replay sample. Empirically, this regularizer is applied with a small coefficient ( λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 ) and we observe that it is sufficient to stabilize ratio learning throughout training.

sections.heading: G.4 Computation and Memory Cost
sections.text: We report the GPU memory allocation and total training time in Table 4 . All measurements are obtained on a desktop workstation with an Intel Xeon Gold 6242R CPU, 376 GB memory, and an NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Although DoobPPO and DoobGRPO are not the most lightweight methods in terms of raw memory or wall-clock time, their computational overhead remains moderate and is comparable to several strong diffusion-policy baselines. In particular, DoobPPO requires 1578 MB GPU memory and 25.28 minutes, while DoobGRPO requires 1795 MB and 28.12 minutes, both remaining in the same practical regime as DPMD, DACER, and SDAC. Considering that our methods achieve state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on most benchmark tasks, these results indicate a favorable performance–efficiency trade-off. Overall, DoobPO delivers stronger empirical performance without incurring prohibitive computational or memory cost. sections.heading: Ablation Study on Ratio Network Size.
sections.text: We study the sensitivity of DoobPPO to the ratio-network architecture on HalfCheetah-v4 . We compare three variants: an MLP ratio network with 3 layers of width 256, a deeper MLP with 10 layers of width 256, and a larger ResNet-style architecture with 20 layers of width 512. As shown in Figure 3 , the simple 3 × \times 256 MLP achieves the best performance, consistently outperforming both the deeper MLP and the larger ResNet-style model. This suggests that increasing the capacity of the ratio network does not necessarily improve performance, and may even make optimization less effective. Based on this result, we use the 3 × \times 256 MLP ratio network in all diffusion-policy experiments.

sections.heading: Ablation Study on Diffusion Steps.
sections.text: We also study the sensitivity of DoobPPO to the number of diffusion steps on HalfCheetah-v4 . We compare three settings, namely T = 10 T=10 , T = 20 T=20 , and T = 30 T=30 . The results show that T = 20 T=20 achieves the best overall performance, while T = 10 T=10 remains competitive but consistently underperforms T = 20 T=20 , and T = 30 T=30 leads to a substantial degradation. These results suggest that DoobPO benefits from a moderately sized diffusion process rather than a very shallow or overly long denoising chain. Therefore, we use 20 20 diffusion steps in all diffusion-policy experiments.

sections.heading: Ablation Study on Ratio Network Size.
sections.text: We study the sensitivity of DoobGRPO to the ratio-network architecture on HalfCheetah-v4 with flow policies. We compare the same three variants as in the diffusion-policy setting: an MLP ratio network with 3 layers of width 256, a deeper MLP with 10 layers of width 256, and a ResNet-style architecture with 20 blocks of width 512. As shown in Figure 4 (a), the simple 3 × \times 256 MLP achieves the best performance with a peak return of 6433, while both the deeper MLP (peak return 23) and the larger ResNet (peak return − - 94) fail to learn meaningful policies. This is consistent with the diffusion-policy ablation, confirming that a lightweight ratio network is critical for stable training across both generative-model backbones.

sections.heading: Ablation Study on Flow Steps.
sections.text: We also study the sensitivity of DoobGRPO to the number of flow integration steps on HalfCheetah-v4 . We compare T = 10 T=10 , T = 20 T=20 , and T = 30 T=30 . As shown in Figure 4 (b), the default setting T = 20 T=20 achieves the best peak performance (6433), while T = 10 T=10 (6120) and T = 30 T=30 (6282) remain competitive but slightly underperform T = 20 T=20 . These results suggest that DoobPO is relatively robust to the choice of flow steps, with T = 20 T=20 providing the best trade-off between sampling quality and computational cost. We use 20 20 flow steps in all flow-policy experiments.

Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for robotic and sequential decision-making systems. However, their action likelihoods are generally intractable, limiting the direct use of widely adopted policy optimization methods such as PPO and GRPO. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO), a framework that leverages Doob’s h h -transform for likelihood-free reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative policies. DoobPO separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. It first learns a lightweight ratio model that represents the desired policy update, and then distills the resulting ratio-tilted target policy into the generative policy via conditional drift matching. This formulation applies uniformly to both diffusion and flow policies and supports a broad family of policy improvement rules, including PPO and GRPO. We prove that the practical conditional drift matching objective is gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective. We further show that the induced diffusion process solves an endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem. This establishes that it achieves the minimum-energy modification required to realize the desired policy tilt. Across MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, DoobPO achieves strong performance against competitive diffusion- and flow-policy baselines, showing a principled and practical route to RL fine-tuning for generative policies. 1 Introduction Generative policies based on diffusion models ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) and flow matching models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for policy learning. Diffusion policies generate actions through iterative denoising, while flow policies generate actions by integrating a learned velocity field, often providing a deterministic and more efficient alternative. Due to their flexibility and accuracy in modeling high-dimensional action distributions, generative policies have achieved strong empirical gains over deterministic or unimodal policies in challenging continuous-control settings ( Ke et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . A natural way to further improve generative policies is through reinforcement learning fine-tuning. However, a central challenge is that the exact likelihoods of generative policies are generally intractable, since each action is produced only after simulating an entire denoising or flow trajectory. This prevents the direct use of many stable and widely adopted policy optimization methods, such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Several recent works have attempted to bypass this likelihood challenge ( Psenka et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; McAllister et al., 2025 ) . However, these methods often suffer from biased estimation, limited data efficiency, substantial computational overhead, or restriction to a particular generative policy class or policy update rule. Consequently, the full potential of RL for diffusion and flow policies remains underexplored. To address this problem, we propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO) , a likelihood-free framework that separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. The first stage represents the desired policy improvement through a target policy ratio. The second stage distills the resulting ratio-tilted target into the generative policy. This decomposition avoids evaluating the likelihood of the generative policy itself. The policy-improvement stage is agnostic to the underlying generative model and accommodates a broad family of updates, including regularized Policy Mirror Descent ( Zhan et al., 2023 ) , Soft Actor-Critic ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) , PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . The generative stage uses Doob’s h h -transform to characterize the ratio-tilted target process and learns this process through Doob’s Drift Matching. The same construction applies to both diffusion and flow policies. Contributions. Our contributions are three-fold: • Method. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO) , a unified framework for RL fine-tuning of generative policies without evaluating exact action likelihoods ( Section 3 ). DoobPO follows a two-stage design: it first obtains the target policy ratio and then transfers the resulting policy improvement into the generative policy through a tractable conditional drift matching objective. The framework supports both diffusion and flow policies ( Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). We summarize the procedures in Algorithms 1 and 2 . Instantiating DoobPO with different policy updates yields DoobPMD , DoobPPO , and DoobGRPO . We further show that several existing methods arise as special cases under particular choices of the policy update and generative policy class ( Section 3.3 ). We summarize these instantiations in Table 1 . • Theory. We characterize the ratio-tilted target policy through Doob’s h h -transform ( Lemma 3.1 ). This characterization leads to Doob’s Drift Matching as a principled way to realize the desired policy update. For tractability, we introduce a conditional drift matching objective and prove that its gradient is proportional to that of the ideal Doob’s Drift Matching objective for both diffusion and flow policies ( Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 ). From the Stochastic Optimal Control perspective ( Section 3.4 ), we further show that the Doob-transformed diffusion solves the corresponding endpoint-constrained control problem ( Proposition 3.1 ). Hence, DoobPO learns the minimum-energy modification of the pretrained diffusion process that realizes the terminal tilt ( Remark 3.2 ). • Experiments. We evaluate DoobPO on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks with both diffusion and flow policies ( Section 4 ). For diffusion policies, DoobPO achieves the strongest overall performance against competitive diffusion-policy RL baselines, with leading results on most tasks ( Section 4.2 ). For flow policies, DoobGRPO achieves the best performance on 9 out of 10 tasks under the same interaction budget and delivers large gains on challenging locomotion environments ( Section 4.3 ). These results establish DoobPO as a strong and practical framework for RL fine-tuning across both diffusion and flow policies. Notation. We summarize notation and time conventions in Appendix A . The first is the generative policy class. The second is the policy update method that specifies the target policy improvement. Different choices along these two dimensions induce a broad family of diffusion/flow matching RL algorithms. Under this view, several prior methods arise as special cases of DoobPO. In particular, they correspond to policy updates that admit closed-form solutions. In these cases, the ratio-learning stage becomes unnecessary, and DoobPO reduces to a single reweighted drift matching step. For example, DPMD ( Ma et al., 2025 ) corresponds to a policy update with an analytic target ratio. Under a KL-proximal policy mirror descent update ( Zhan et al., 2023 ) , the updated policy satisfies π ⁡ ( a | o ) ∝ π old ​ ( a | o ) ​ exp ⁡ ( A ^ old ​ ( o , a ) / λ ) \pi(a|o)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a|o)\exp(\hat{A}_{\mathrm{old}}(o,a)/\lambda) . For more general trust-region policy-gradient methods such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , the target ratio does not admit a closed form.
